hints: Notice the column headings increase in wavelength from $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ on the left to $10^{2}\text{ m}$ on the right, a range of 16 orders of magnitude.
Recall the EM spectrum in order of increasing wavelength: gamma ray, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infra-red, microwave, radio wave.
Compare the middle $10^{-6}\text{ m}$ column with visible light at about $10^{-7}\text{ m}$ to decide whether infra-red or ultraviolet fits there.
walkthrough: List the given wavelengths in order: $10^{-14}\text{ m}$, $10^{-10}\text{ m}$, $10^{-6}\text{ m}$, $10^{-2}\text{ m}$, $10^{2}\text{ m}$.

State the EM spectrum order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays shortest at about $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-12}\text{ m}$, then X-rays about $10^{-12}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-8}\text{ m}$, then ultraviolet and visible near $10^{-8}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-6}\text{ m}$, then infra-red near $10^{-6}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-3}\text{ m}$, then microwaves near $10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-1}\text{ m}$, then radio waves longest.

Match each value: $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ is principal gamma radiation, $10^{-10}\text{ m}$ is principal X-ray radiation, $10^{-6}\text{ m}$ is just beyond visible so principal infra-red, $10^{-2}\text{ m}$ is principal microwave, $10^{2}\text{ m}$ is principal radio wave.
Check distractors: any row starting with radio wave at $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ reverses the spectrum, and ultraviolet does not belong at $10^{-6}\text{ m}$.
This sequence gamma ray, X-ray, infra-red, microwave, radio wave is row A. This is option A.

A.explanation: Matches the spectrum order: $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ gamma ray, $10^{-10}\text{ m}$ X-ray, $10^{-6}\text{ m}$ infra-red, $10^{-2}\text{ m}$ microwave, $10^{2}\text{ m}$ radio wave.

B.explanation: Reverses short and long wavelength ends and puts X-ray at $10^{-2}\text{ m}$, which is a microwave wavelength.

C.explanation: Reverses the order and misplaces ultraviolet at $10^{-6}\text{ m}$ and X-ray at $10^{2}\text{ m}$.

D.explanation: Puts X-ray at $10^{-14}\text{ m}$ and infra-red at $10^{-10}\text{ m}$, both too short by several orders of magnitude.
